description: Adversarial Wave 0 (translation sprint 459) over the 219 new-and-changed lpn_ keys reported by wave0_keyset.php --new-and-changed --prefix=lpn (3 of 222 in-scope keys pre-filtered as already carrying a non-empty $ec_lang_syn). The question asked of every string was NOT 'is this good?' but 'list every plausible reading; if there is more than one, propose a rewrite.' Special attention paid to the search and terrain consent dialogs per the task brief. Result: 11 findings -- 8 english, 1 english (consistency), 3 dismissed, 1 refer-to-human. Every entry is open in the sense that this pass proposes; it does not write $ec_lang or $ec_lang_syn. | Wave 0 findings ruled and applied 2026-08-24: eight English rewrites in lib/lang.ec.en.php, one referred key resolved from the code, ONE still open for Tom (the two orphan *_syn keys). The three consent-dialog findings were the important ones and all three are in the two permission dialogs Task 507 had just keyed.

entries.complaint: high: 'Options for units change:' has two parses -- a noun phrase 'options for [a units change]' (heading over the nondestructive/destructive choice that follows, the intended reading) and a clause 'options for units [change]', i.e. the options themselves change. The compressed noun-pile makes 'change' read as a verb on first pass.
readings: the choices available for how a unit change is carried out (intended)
the available unit options are changing / have changed
entries.resolution: APPLIED 2026-08-24: 'Options for units change:' -> 'When you change a unit:'.

entries.complaint: high: 'variable storage depending on variable levels' is circular -- it defines a tank's storage as depending on its own levels without saying what varies or why, and repeating 'variable' twice gives a translator nothing concrete to render. Its sibling lpn_tool_add_reservoir_tip ('an infinite source with a fixed water level') is concrete and parallel; this one is not.
readings: storage whose water level rises and falls as it fills and drains (intended)
storage of a variable, unspecified amount, that happens to depend on levels that are also variable (no concrete picture)
entries.resolution: APPLIED 2026-08-24: '...variable storage depending on variable levels' -> '...storage whose water level rises and falls as it fills and empties'. The old wording used one word twice to define itself.

entries.complaint: medium: 'These parts as a table you can sort.' is a sentence fragment -- it has a subject and two noun phrases but no verb, so 'as' has to be silently read as 'shown as' or 'presented as'. A translator without a strong intuition for English ellipsis has no verb to anchor a translation on.
readings: These parts, shown as a table you can sort (intended)
not parseable as a complete sentence without inference
entries.resolution: APPLIED 2026-08-24: 'These parts as a table' -> 'These parts shown as a table' -- the missing verb.

entries.complaint: high: the second sentence, 'Self-sets intelligently sometimes.', has no recoverable subject or object. It is not clear what 'self-sets' (mode? a property? a value?), what makes it 'intelligent', or what 'sometimes' is conditioned on. This is the strongest single finding in the set -- an English reader has no plausible single reading, only a guess.
readings: unrecoverable -- no antecedent for 'self' and no stated object for 'sets'
entries.resolution: APPLIED 2026-08-24, after reading what the code actually does. 'Self-sets intelligently sometimes' names seven `setMode('select')` call sites: opening a project or an example, clearing the network, restoring a georeferenced project, and the fat-finger rule (a tap in an Add mode that lands on something already there opens it instead of stacking a duplicate). Rewritten to 'The page comes back to this mode by itself after some actions, such as opening a project.' -- honest, translatable, and it names the case a user will actually meet rather than claiming intelligence.

entries.complaint: medium: 'Water quality is not modeled. Valves are: a throttle valve works in either solver, and...' -- 'Valves are:' promises a list or a definition after the colon, but what follows is a full compound sentence, not a completion of 'Valves are'. The colon creates a false expectation of a predicate.
readings: Valves [behave as follows]: a throttle valve works in either solver... (intended)
Valves are: [some property or list] -- syntactically broken, no completion follows
entries.resolution: APPLIED 2026-08-24: 'Valves are:' -> 'Valves:' -- the colon carries it; the verb promised a completion that never came.

entries.complaint: medium: 'Step 2 of 2 — fine' uses 'fine' in its precision sense (paired with 'Step 1 of 2 — quick' and lpn_georef_intro's 'Step 2 is the fine one'), but this label is rendered standalone as a short step indicator, decontextualized from the paragraph that anchors that sense. 'Fine' is one of English's most common polysemy traps -- its everyday sense is 'okay/satisfactory', which is nonsensical here but plausible enough to make a translator hesitate or guess wrong, especially since 'fine=precise' is a lower-frequency sense than 'fine=OK' or 'fine=weather'.
readings: the fine (precise, detailed) step, as opposed to the quick one (intended)
Step 2 of 2 -- [status:] fine / OK
fine as in weather, irrelevant but momentarily available
entries.resolution: APPLIED 2026-08-24: 'Step 2 of 2 - fine' -> 'Step 2 of 2 - precise'. Pairs with step 1's 'quick', which is the contrast the two steps actually are, and drops the everyday 'fine = OK' reading entirely.

entries.complaint: high (consent dialog): 'They will receive your search words and your IP address.' -- 'They' has no clean antecedent inside this string; the service name (nominatim.openstreetmap.org / OpenStreetMap Foundation) was named two sentences earlier in the PRECEDING key (lpn_search_consent_1), a separate translation unit a translator may render out of that exact sequence. The parallel terrain dialog names the recipient explicitly in the analogous sentence ('Mapbox will receive those coordinates and your IP address.') -- this key is the one place in the two consent flows that relies on a pronoun instead. A consent string that names who receives your data should not depend on grammatical memory across two separately-translated strings, and pronoun gender/number agreement in many target languages depends on which antecedent a translator infers.
readings: the place-name service / Nominatim / OpenStreetMap Foundation will receive... (intended, but not stated in this string)
the street map pictures mentioned in the previous sentence will receive...
no antecedent recoverable if this string is read alone
entries.resolution: APPLIED 2026-08-24: 'They will receive' -> 'The place-name service will receive', matching the terrain dialog's pattern of naming the recipient. In a consent dialog a pronoun with no antecedent is not a wording defect, it is a consent defect.

entries.complaint: high (consent dialog): 'May we use it?' -- this is the literal permission question the Accept/Reject buttons answer, and 'it' has no clean noun antecedent in the immediately preceding sentence ('...we keep no record of your searches.' -- 'searches' is plural, and 'it' cannot idiomatically refer back to it). The nearest singular candidates are 'the place-name service' (consent_1) or 'a search' (consent_2), both distant and both requiring the reader to reconstruct across string boundaries. This is exactly the class of ambiguity the brief calls out: the reader may correctly consent without being sure what they consented to.
readings: May we send your searches to the place-name service? (intended)
May we use your search words / your IP address?
May we use your searches (the record we said we don't keep)?
entries.resolution: APPLIED 2026-08-24: 'May we use it?' -> 'May we send your searches to the place-name service?' Names both the thing sent and who gets it, so the question stands alone.

entries.complaint: high (consent dialog): same defect as lpn_search_consent_3 -- 'May we use it?' with no antecedent in the immediately preceding sentence, which ends '...nothing is stored on this device except your answer to this question.' The nearest singular candidate ('Mapbox') is two sentences back. Both consent flows share this exact string, which means the ambiguity is systemic to the pattern, not a one-off typo.
readings: May we send your node positions to Mapbox? (intended)
May we use your node positions / your IP address?
unclear antecedent if read as the standalone consent question it functionally is
entries.resolution: APPLIED 2026-08-24: 'May we use it?' -> 'May we send your node positions to Mapbox?' Same fix, same reason.

entries.complaint: low: 'Credits' as a bare link label could plausibly be read as financial credit rather than attribution/acknowledgement. Flagging because a later reviewer skimming this key in isolation (outside the code comment that explains it) would likely re-flag it.
readings: acknowledgement of the color-ramp scheme's source/author (intended)
a financial credit or account balance
entries.resolution: Dismissed -- js/looped-network.js:~8330-8338 documents this as a deliberate word choice (Tom, 2026-08-20: 'THE WORD IS "Credits", NOT "About"' -- 'About' sounds like a Help link). 'Credits' in a software-attribution context is the dominant established UI sense; leaving as-is.

entries.complaint: low: 'Replace those {n} with the land surface?' literally reads as replacing a value with a physical object rather than with an elevation reading taken from it. Only one plausible reading survives once the preceding string (lpn_terrain_confirm_default_1) is read first, since these two strings are always shown together as one dialog.
readings: replace those elevations with elevations read from the land surface (intended, recoverable from context)
replace the nodes themselves with the land surface (not a serious competing reading given context)
entries.resolution: Dismissed -- always rendered directly under lpn_terrain_confirm_default_1, which supplies 'elevation' as the object being replaced; no realistic second reading in situ.

entries.complaint: process finding, not a wording defect: lpn_profile_tip_syn and lpn_profile_title_syn are ordinary $ec_lang keys (not entries in the off-limits $ec_lang_syn array) with no call site anywhere in js/ or *.php -- grep found them only in lang files and generated payloads. They read like synonym-rich variants of lpn_profile_tip / lpn_profile_title that were meant to go into $ec_lang_syn (which is exactly the payload shape: 'Draw the ground or grade... path, route, or way...') but were instead committed as their own translatable $ec_lang keys. As written, sprint 459 is about to pay for full sentence translations, in 26 languages, of two strings nothing displays.
readings: leftover/misfiled content meant for $ec_lang_syn (most likely)
a genuinely unwired future call site (dead for now, intentionally parked)
entries.resolution: RULED AND APPLIED 2026-08-24. Tom: "there is a tip on Profile menu and Profile tab, identical. In other words, these are real strings. And these _syns are really needed. Are they simply keyed wrong? I guess 1. My mistake." -- which is the written permission $ec_lang_syn requires, and it also settles the confusion: lpn_profile_tip and lpn_profile_title ARE rendered (the menu row and the pane tab share one tip); it was only the _syn twins that nothing displayed. Both moved verbatim into $ec_lang_syn beside the keys they describe, and the two orphan $ec_lang keys deleted. No sprint now pays to translate a string nobody sees, and the synonyms reach translators through the channel written for them.

entries.complaint: A JS-concatenated fragment (tileCount + ' ' + string), which fixes the number to the FRONT of the sentence; Turkish wants it after the noun phrase. Bengali filed the same complaint independently for a different reason -- its numeral classifier টি must attach directly to the numeral, and concatenation put a space between them.
readings: a tail fragment juxtaposed after a bare number, accepting reduced fluency
a whole sentence with {n}, like its own siblings lpn_terrain_done and lpn_terrain_missed
entries.resolution: FIXED 2026-08-24, mid-sprint. English became '{n} request(s) to api.mapbox.com.' and js/lpn-terrain.js substitutes it, keeping the old concatenation as a fallback for a value with no {n}. TWO LANGUAGES, TWO UNRELATED GRAMMARS, ONE STRING -- the English-source signal, and the tell was visible without either: this was the only counted string on that dialog whose siblings had a placeholder and it did not. The 19 languages already written were repaired by prefixing '{n} ', which reproduces the previous rendering character for character; Bengali got '{n}টি' with no space, as its agent had explained. COST OF THE TIMING: the payloads were built before the edit, so nine later agents met a payload disagreeing with the source. Do not edit the English while agents are reading a payload built from it -- a mid-sprint finding waits for close.

entries.complaint: The pt glossary maps both 'default' and 'pattern' to 'padrão', so a literal composition reads 'Padrão de demanda padrão' -- a doubled word that reads like a typo.
readings: Padrão de demanda predefinido (used)
Padrão de demanda padrão (literal, awkward)
entries.resolution: Dismissed as an ENGLISH defect: an English reader does not stumble on 'Default demand pattern', so by the routing rule this is not an English case. The agent's own fix -- 'predefinido' for default here -- is right and is kept. Recorded rather than silently closed because the collision is a standing property of Portuguese and will recur on any future key pairing those two words; a glossary note for pt is the place to settle it if it does.

entries.complaint: Says 'lon/lat' while the sibling flow (lpn_goto_menu, 'Go to a latitude and longitude') and its own neighbour lpn_georef_asdegrees ('a longitude and a latitude') use the other order; the reversed order reads like a copy-paste variant rather than a deliberate distinction.
readings: the same concept as lat/lon elsewhere, translated in the established order
literally lon/lat, producing an order inconsistency across three sibling strings
entries.resolution: OPEN for Tom. The two orders are both defensible -- lon/lat is x-then-y and matches how a file's coordinates are actually stored, lat/lon is how people say it -- and the button is about what is IN the file, so the reversal may well be deliberate. It is a wording call on a control, which is his. Note it sits beside the unresolved mode-name question below.

entries.complaint: Bare 'Credits' with no object stated; could mean attribution for the map tiles or for the colour scheme. Had to read the surrounding source lines to confirm it is the latter.
readings: colour-scheme attribution
map-tile source attribution
entries.resolution: Dismissed, and this is the second time: the word is a documented deliberate choice in js/looped-network.js and was already dismissed in the sprint-459 Wave 0 pass for the same reason. The German agent reached it independently and resolved it correctly from context in one step, which is the evidence that the context does the work. If a third language files it, that is the threshold to revisit.
